solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Lose everything, presumably, being a dipsomaniac

parts.note: turned into its opposite: the flip side of losing
likewise flipped to nothing, which is the zero-shaped letter O

explanation.surface: A heavy drinker who, it seems, has lost everything to the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay works by opposites: if you lose everything, presumably you win nothing, and O stands for zero.
explanation.definitionFit: A wino is a slang name for a habitual drunk, which is exactly what a dipsomaniac suffers from being.

clue.text: Wager involving everyone in Swan Lake, for example

indicators.note: something that involves another thing takes it inside itself, so one piece wraps another

explanation.surface: A bet in which everyone takes part, placed at a performance of Swan Lake.
explanation.walkthrough: "Swan Lake, for example" is a definition by example; the surface makes it sound like the place where the bet is laid.
explanation.definitionFit: Swan Lake is Tchaikovsky's famous dance work, one example of the classical theatrical form performed by trained dancers.

clue.text: Fellow having wander round back of big tree

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, so one piece is placed outside another
the back of a word is its final letter, so only the last one is kept

explanation.surface: A man goes for a stroll around the far side of a large tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The container works on the charade already built, so "round" wraps the first two pieces together around the last letter of big, which slots in at their join.
explanation.definitionFit: The mangrove is a tropical tree growing in coastal swamps, one particular kind of the general woody plant.

clue.text: Norse god — initially only deity in Norway

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word gives up just its opening letter

parts.note: first letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A Norse god described as the only deity in Norway.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition and the wordplay's subject overlap so neatly that the clue nearly reads as an &lit.
explanation.definitionFit: Odin is the chief deity of Scandinavian mythology, ruler of Asgard and father of Thor.

clue.text: Loan shark certain to reside in ancient city

indicators.note: whatever resides in a place lives inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: Ur is the ancient Sumerian city, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A loan shark who is sure to settle in some ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: Ur, the Sumerian city in modern Iraq, is a crossword regular because its two letters are so handy.
explanation.definitionFit: A usurer lends money at exorbitant interest rates, just as a loan shark does; the terms are synonyms.

clue.text: Perk up, hearing of south coast resort

indicators.note: hearing something rather than seeing it written means only its sound counts

parts.note: Brighton is a seaside town on England's south coast

explanation.surface: Someone cheers up on hearing news of a seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: Brighton, the English seaside town in Sussex, is pronounced the same as the verb meaning cheer up.
explanation.definitionFit: To brighten is to become more cheerful or lively, which is the intransitive sense of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: Chirpy type taking notes in US intelligence

indicators.note: to take something is to take it in, so one piece holds another

parts.note: three musical notes, C, A and D

explanation.surface: A cheerful spy taking notes while working for American intelligence.
explanation.walkthrough: "Chirpy" looks like cheerful, but here it is literal: the creature chirps. Musical notes can be any of the letters A to G.
explanation.definitionFit: The cicada is an insect famous for its loud shrill chirping song, making it a cryptic description of a noisy creature.

clue.text: Wish of French teacher, possibly, to take English

parts.note: British schoolchildren address a male teacher as sir

explanation.surface: What a French teacher might hope for when taking on an English class.
explanation.walkthrough: "French teacher" reads as one unit, but "of French" is the first piece and the teacher is separate.
explanation.definitionFit: A desire is a strong longing or craving, so the noun is a plain synonym of a wish.

clue.text: Lout spilling oil in Native American hut

indicators.note: spilt liquid ends up splashed about in no fixed order
one thing being in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: a hogan is a traditional Navajo dwelling

explanation.surface: A lout spilling oil inside a Native American hut.
explanation.walkthrough: The Navajo hut is less familiar than wigwam or tepee, so the fodder is easier to spot than the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A hooligan is a rowdy, violent young troublemaker, a direct synonym of lout.

clue.text: Right time of life for fashion

parts.note: a person's age is their time of life

explanation.surface: The right stage in life to take an interest in fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: "Rage" means fashion in the phrase "all the rage".
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is the current craze or vogue is called the rage, a sense close to a fashion or trend.

clue.text: Crossing river, arrived at small cave

indicators.note: to cross something is to stretch over it from side to side, so one piece spans another

parts.note: got to, as in reached a place

explanation.surface: A traveller crosses a river and comes upon a small cave.
explanation.walkthrough: "Crossing river" looks like the traveller's journey, but it tells GOT TO to straddle R.
explanation.definitionFit: A grotto is a small picturesque cavern, often artificial, so the noun matches a little hollow in rock.

clue.text: European working in a manor

indicators.note: something being worked is kneaded and reshaped, so the letters take a new order

explanation.surface: A European employed as staff in a country house.
explanation.walkthrough: "Working" seems to describe the European's job, but it tells you to rearrange the following letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A Romanian is a citizen of Romania in south-eastern Europe, so is one specific example of a European.

clue.text: Wading bird biting head off rue?

indicators.note: biting off a head removes the front, so the first letter goes

explanation.surface: A wading bird biting the top off rue, a bitter herb.
explanation.walkthrough: Rue looks like the herb the bird is eating, but it is the verb meaning regret; drop the R.
explanation.definitionFit: The egret is a white heron found in marshes, one kind of long-legged bird that feeds in shallow water.

clue.text: Eastern vacation ultimately feasible, much to be desired

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

explanation.surface: An Eastern holiday that at last seems possible, and is very desirable.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an adjectival phrase: something much to be desired.
explanation.definitionFit: Something enviable arouses envy because others would like it too, so it is highly desirable.

clue.text: The vehicle in front?

definitions.meaning: a covered motor vehicle used for carrying goods
the shortened form of vanguard, the leading part of an army or movement

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the familiar driving phrase "the vehicle in front"; to be in the van is to be at the forefront.
explanation.definitionFit: Van is both a goods lorry and the shortened form of vanguard, the leading position of a moving group.

clue.text: Reflect about old Mickey, perhaps

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is placed round another

explanation.surface: Thinking back fondly about the old Mickey of cartoons.
explanation.walkthrough: MUSE opens after its M to take O.
explanation.definitionFit: Mickey is Disney's famous cartoon rodent, so he is one example of the small animal, hence the "perhaps".

clue.text: Like rough ground? That's odd

definitions.meaning: rough ground is bumpy, not level
an odd number cannot be divided by two

explanation.surface: Someone puzzled about whether a patch of ground is rough.
explanation.walkthrough: "That's odd" reads as surprise, but odd is the number sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Bumpy terrain is not level, and numbers like three and seven are not even, so one word covers both.

clue.text: Scandinavian invader's female ruler

parts.note: Vi, short for Violet, is a woman's name

explanation.surface: The woman who ruled over a Scandinavian raider.
explanation.walkthrough: "Female ruler" looks like a queen, but the two words are separate pieces, a girl's name and a male monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vikings were Norse seafaring raiders who attacked and settled much of northern Europe in the early medieval period.

clue.text: Tawdry gear used by school

explanation.surface: Cheap-looking equipment used by a school.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English kit is the gear or uniform used for a sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Kitsch describes art or objects in cheap, showy, sentimental bad taste, which is the sense of tawdry.

clue.text: Stake in metropolitan tenement

indicators.note: in means contained within, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: the end of metropolitan and start of tenement

explanation.surface: A financial stake held in a city apartment block.
explanation.walkthrough: "Stake" suggests property ownership, but the poker sense is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker the ante is the bet each player must put into the pot before the deal.

clue.text: Blandishments from cook drinking coffee

indicators.note: whoever drinks something takes it inside, so one piece swallows another

parts.note: a latte is a milky coffee

explanation.surface: A chef sipping coffee lays on the sweet talk.
explanation.walkthrough: "Cook" looks like a noun, the chef, but it is the verb, and a milky Italian coffee is the drink swallowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Flattery is excessive insincere praise meant to win favour, which is exactly what blandishments are.

clue.text: Finance duke used to support entertainment

explanation.surface: A duke's money is used to back some entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the supporting piece goes underneath, so D follows FUN.
explanation.definitionFit: To fund something is to provide money for it, a direct synonym of the verb finance.

clue.text: Genuine-sounding Scottish dance

indicators.note: sounding like something means matching it in pronunciation, not spelling

explanation.surface: A dance that seems authentically Scottish.
explanation.walkthrough: "Genuine-sounding" looks like a description of the dance but is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The reel is a lively traditional folk dance of Scotland, performed in lines or sets to fast music.

clue.text: Seabird circling a very public house

indicators.note: circling something means going all round it, so one piece surrounds another

explanation.surface: A seabird flying round a pub that is very public indeed.
explanation.walkthrough: "Very public house" reads as one phrase, but very is a piece and the definition is just public house.
explanation.definitionFit: A tavern is an inn or bar selling alcohol, and a public house is the British term for a pub.

clue.text: Be without the old retired valet

parts.note: to be without something is to lack it

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing or going back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: ye is the archaic form of the

explanation.surface: Being without the old valet who has now retired.
explanation.walkthrough: "Retired valet" looks like a pensioned servant, but retired acts on the piece before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A lackey is a liveried manservant or footman, so a servant like a valet.
